verdict.summary: In PlayerGeneric::~PlayerGeneric, `mixer` is deleted at line 4 if non-NULL, then dereferenced unconditionally at line 8 (`mixer->isActive() && !mixer->isDeviceRemoved(player)`) with no NULL or validity check in between. If `mixer` was NULL at entry (a state the fragment itself anticipates via `if (mixer)` at line 3), line 8 is a NULL-pointer dereference (CWE-476); if it was non-NULL, line 4 frees it and line 8 dereferences freed memory (CWE-416). The absent one-statement fix is a NULL/validity guard on `mixer` before the line-8 dereference, e.g. `if (mixer && mixer->isActive() && ...)`.

evidence.reason: `mixer` is dereferenced at line 8 without any guard between line 3 and the use. Line 3 `if (mixer)` demonstrates `mixer`'s value domain includes NULL, and its false branch delivers mixer==NULL straight to line 8; on its true branch, `delete mixer;` at line 4 frees the object and line 8 dereferences the dangling pointer. Line 6 `if (player)` admits player!=NULL and imposes no constraint on `mixer`, so no shown guard excludes either failure value. The line-3 `if (mixer)` fails the Guard-Identity Audit: it constrains the delete, not the dereference (wrong-target drift), and the intervening delete mutates the pointer between check and use (check-then-use drift). The absent fix form is a NULL/validity check on `mixer` before the line-8 dereference (e.g., `mixer &&` prepended to the condition); its absence leaves NULL dereference (CWE-476, primary) and use-after-free (CWE-416, secondary) at this sink.

assumptions: `mixer` and `player` are pointer members; the fragment itself treats `mixer` as possibly NULL via `if (mixer)` at line 3 and `player` via `if (player)` at line 6.
No statement in the fragment links player!=NULL to mixer!=NULL, so the entry states mixer==NULL and mixer!=NULL can both coincide with the `if (player)` block.
limitations: `mixer->removeDevice(player)` at line 9 is also an unprotected dereference, but it is unreachable in every confirmed failure because `mixer->isActive()` at line 8 already faults; it is shadowed by the line-8 finding.

The exact NULL/non-NULL construction state of `mixer` originates outside the fragment; the fragment's own NULL check at line 3 and the `delete mixer;` at line 4 are the in-fragment evidence that both states reach line 8.

Whether the destructor crash is remotely/attacker-triggerable depends on call sites outside the fragment; the verdict rests on the failure being producible from entry states that the fragment's own guards admit.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability. The only attacker-controlled values that reach dangerous operations are sent to bounded, literal-format sinks: the option-append calls carry an explicit OPTSMAX bound and the buffers are zero-initialized (lines 66, 71, 116, 126), every fprintf uses a literal format with at most a matching %s (lines 58, 153, 163), the malloc result is NULL-checked before use (line 57), and the sole argv index is guarded by the loop condition (line 151). verdict.summary: openssl_encrypt computes the output buffer size at line 36 as outlen = data_len + EVP_CIPHER_block_size(cipher_type) with no bound on the entry-point-derived data_len (parsed at line 12). For data_len > INT_MAX - block_size the signed int addition wraps, and the wrapped value is used as the emalloc size at line 37 and as the sizing basis for the EVP_EncryptUpdate write at line 44, giving an integer-overflow-corrupted allocation size (CWE-190) with potential heap buffer overflow of the ciphertext buffer (CWE-787). No guard between line 12 and line 36 constrains data_len: line 16 checks only the cipher lookup, line 22 and line 40 check password length, line 31 is a warning on iv_len (wrong-target drift for each). The wrapped outlen is consumed at line 37 as the emalloc size, the CWE-190 corrupted-allocation-size sink; the absent fix statement is a bound rejection of data_len > INT_MAX - EVP_CIPHER_block_size(cipher_type) before this addition.

The write consumes the attacker-controlled data_len (up to type maximum) into the buffer whose capacity was computed from the overflowed outlen at lines 36-37; with no bound check on data_len anywhere on the path, the ciphertext output (up to ~data_len + block_size bytes per EVP_EncryptUpdate/EVP_EncryptFinal semantics) can exceed or misrelate to the corrupted allocation, the CWE-787 heap-overflow mechanism downstream of the CWE-190 size corruption. Surviving witness data_len = INT_MAX passes every guard (lines 16, 22, 31, 40 all constrain different values); absent fix: rejection of data_len > INT_MAX - EVP_CIPHER_block_size(cipher_type) before line 36.

assumptions: The cipher selected via method has EVP_CIPHER_block_size >= 1 (e.g., 16 for aes-256-cbc reachable through EVP_get_cipherbyname at line 15).

limitations: The exact physical heap-corruption step depends on emalloc behavior with the wrapped size: on 64-bit builds the wrapped negative outlen+1 converts to an enormous size and typically terminates fatally (crash-only DoS, demoted); the confirmed mechanism is the integer-overflow-corrupted allocation size consumed at lines 37 and 44.
php_openssl_validate_iv at line 34 is not shown, so the IV-padding path and the discarded-return nuance cannot be confirmed as a finding from this fragment.
Whether a data string of length INT_MAX is practically allocatable depends on memory available to the PHP process, but the length value itself is directly supplied by the entry-point argument.

The descriptor boundary check at lines 98-99 (admitted set offset_x+width <= gif->width and offset_y+height <= gif->height) exactly constrains the scanline writes at lines 264/283 and the clear-branch memsets at lines 305-313; the byte-count guards at lines 67, 117, 150, 177 and the trailer early-exit at line 185 bound every gif_data read; bitmap_get_buffer results are NULL-checked (lines 164-165, 241-242); lzw_decode_init/lzw_decode results are checked (lines 253, 289-297); gif_skip_frame_extensions is checked (line 58). verdict.summary: Out-of-bounds write: filename = string_nextinlist(...) (line 10) copies a config-list item into big_buffer, admitting length up to big_buffer_size-1; suffix = filename + Ustrlen(filename) (line 16) then points at big_buffer's last byte, and the unguarded sprintf calls at lines 25, 30, and 41 append up to ~269 bytes with no length check, overflowing big_buffer (CWE-787). This unguarded sprintf appends ~269 bytes ('.' + %ld up to 11 + '.' + %.256s up to 256 + NUL); for filename length in [big_buffer_size-269, big_buffer_size-1], admitted by every guard on the path (lines 22, 27, 39, 48 — none constrains length), the write exceeds big_buffer: CWE-787. The %.256s width constrains only uts.nodename (Guard-Identity drift: different quantity), and no bound check on the destination write exists; the absent fix is a length guard vs. big_buffer_size or a bounded snprintf.

Same unbounded destination: suffix points at big_buffer[Ustrlen(filename)] (line 16) with filename length up to big_buffer_size-1 (line 10). This write adds up to 257 bytes; for filename length in [big_buffer_size-257, big_buffer_size-1] it overflows big_buffer (CWE-787). No guard on the path constrains the total appended length; %.256s only caps uts.nodename; the missing one-statement fix is a remaining-space/bound check before the write.

Same sink mechanism reached when CONFIGURE_FILE_USE_EUID is defined: filename fills big_buffer to up to big_buffer_size-1 (line 10), suffix points at the final byte (line 16), and this sprintf writes '.', the euid digits, and NUL without any length check, overflowing big_buffer for filename length in [big_buffer_size-12, big_buffer_size-1] (CWE-787). Guards at lines 22/27/39/48 do not constrain filename length; the absent fix form is the added bound check or bounded-write substitution.

assumptions: big_buffer's capacity is big_buffer_size, established by the access convention at line 10 (string_nextinlist called with buffer big_buffer and size big_buffer_size).

string_nextinlist copies the next list item into the supplied buffer, NUL-terminated and truncated to fit big_buffer_size-1 characters, and returns that buffer (name-implied semantics with the shown size argument).
filename returned at line 10 aliases big_buffer, so suffix arithmetic at line 16 positions the appends inside big_buffer.
The preprocessor branches CONFIGURE_FILE_USE_NODE / CONFIGURE_FILE_USE_EUID (lines 15, 20, 24, 38) are part of an analyzed build variant; at least one sprintf branch compiles.
limitations: The witness is a range (filename length near big_buffer_size-1) rather than a single literal; the exact failing list entry is a value the shown code admits but is not displayed as a constant.
Reachability of the OOB write requires a build with CONFIGURE_FILE_USE_NODE and/or CONFIGURE_FILE_USE_EUID defined; the default build may compile the #else branch at lines 53-58.

Possible NULL deref at line 391 (expand_string result used by Ustrtol with no NULL check, unlike lines 236/250/310) is demoted: the NULL producer on this path depends on an unshown expansion-failure condition, which is a generic runtime/config-error trigger rather than a value derivable from the shown statements.
host_number = n (line 400) has no lower-bound check for negative n (only n > LOCALHOST_MAX at line 396); no security-relevant consumer of host_number is shown in the fragment.

Default build analyzed without FEAT_RIGHTLEFT/FEAT_JOB_CHANNEL/FEAT_VARTABS active paths.

Termination of the whitespace-delete (247-249), space-insert (252-268), and replace-restore (156-162) loops depends on callee/virtual-column behavior ('showbreak', 'linebreak', replace-stack drain) not demonstrable in the fragment; no non-termination witness is derivable.

verdict.summary: LogFilePrep passes caller-supplied strings fname and backup directly as the printf-family format argument of asprintf (lines 5 and 15). A value containing conversion specifiers such as %s or %n is interpreted by asprintf, enabling out-of-range argument reads and arbitrary writes (%n), i.e., a format string vulnerability in the X server process. The fix — using the literal format "%s" — is absent on both paths.

evidence.reason: fname is received at line 1 with no content constraint and is used as the format string of the printf-family asprintf sink; the residual range is the full string domain including format directives. A witness like fname="%s" or "%n" reaches the sink with no intervening guard and is interpreted by asprintf, causing calls to read/write memory outside the actual argument list (CWE-134). The absent fix form is the literal-format substitution asprintf(&logFileName, "%s", fname); the only "%s" literal in the fragment (line 16) protects a different call (oldLog), so it does not cover this sink.

backup, constrained only by the non-emptiness check at line 8 (if (backup && *backup)), is used as the format string of asprintf. The line-8 guard admits non-empty strings that still contain conversion specifiers, so a witness like backup="%s" passes it unmodified and is interpreted by asprintf (CWE-134). The absent fix form is asprintf(&suffix, "%s", backup); the literal "%s%s" at line 16 is a different call and does not neutralize this sink.

assumptions: asprintf follows standard printf-family semantics: its second argument is the format string, and conversion directives in it consume/read the supplied varargs or cause reads/writes to memory.
The fragment gives fname and backup no content constraint; their residual ranges are the full C-string domain including '%' directives (line 8 excludes only the empty string for backup).
limitations: No call site of LogFilePrep is shown in the fragment, so whether the caller can truly supply attacker-controlled fname/backup content is established only as the unconstrained parameter domain, not by a shown argv/config source.
The exact memory-corruption payload (e.g., precise %n write target) depends on libc varargs layout and is not demonstrated; the failure is the format interpretation itself.
If a deployment always passes compile-time literal filenames/backups, the flaw is not exploitable, but the fragment imposes no such invariant.

verdict.summary: cmdopts_parse is the protected member of the pair. Every sink whose failure set is demonstrable from the shown statements is guarded by a verbatim protective statement that passes the Guard-Identity Audit: the cmdopts dereferences are unreachable on malloc failure because line 57 checks the return and line 59 exits fail-closed; the read of argv[jas_optind] at line 153 is bounded above by the loop guard at line 150 ('while (jas_optind < argc) {', strict '<', so the last body index is argc-1 and no assignment to jas_optind occurs between the check and the read). The addopt appends (lines 116, 126) are called with an explicit OPTSMAX cap and named-capacity append semantics; the actual buffer size and the callee body are not shown, so no failing value can be demonstrated to reach an unprotected sink. assumptions: argc/argv follow C main semantics: valid indices 0..argc-1.

jas_optind follows the standard getopt convention of being non-negative and only advanced, since its producer jas_getopt is not shown; the fragment itself only adds '++jas_optind' at line 154 after the read.
OPTSMAX is the intended capacity convention for inoptsbuf/outoptsbuf because the fragment passes it as the max argument of addopt at lines 116 and 126.
addopt(buf, max, s) is analyzed by the name-implied standard semantics of a named-capacity append (caps at max), per the call-site confirmation rule.
The jas_getopt table walk terminates at the {-1, 0, 0} sentinel shown at line 51.
limitations: An out-of-bounds write through addopt (lines 116, 126) cannot be confirmed: the declarations of inoptsbuf/outoptsbuf and the body of addopt are not shown, so a claim that OPTSMAX exceeds the real array size or that the callee mis-bounds is an assumed magnitude (demoted per the OOB and Verifiability rules, in both the vulnerable and safe directions).
A negative jas_optind would be admitted by the guard at line 150, but producing it requires the unshown behavior of jas_getopt; argv[-1] is not derivable from any shown statement, so it is demoted.
atoi(jas_optarg) (lines 107, 130) and strtoull(jas_optarg, 0, 10) (line 136) parse attacker-controlled strings, but debug/cmptno/max_mem have no security-relevant consumer shown in this fragment.
If jas_getopt can return a missing-argument state with jas_optarg == NULL, atoi/strtoull/addopt would receive NULL; that producer behavior is not shown, so the NULL-deref candidates are demoted.
Echoing the user's own argv string to stderr (lines 151-153) is a CLI diagnostic write, not a parser-consumed log; no CWE-117 boundary is demonstrated.

verdict.summary: openssl_decrypt() discards the return status of php_base64_decode() at line 30 on the default non-raw path. A failed decode (attacker-supplied invalid base64 in the 'data' parameter) makes line 31 assign data_len from the unchecked/uninitialized base64_str_len (declared line 10) and line 32 set data = base64_str = NULL; these values then reach EVP_DecryptUpdate() at line 54 with no intervening NULL/status check, causing a NULL-pointer dereference/crash (with a possible OOB read window). The absent one-statement fix is a decode-success check such as 'if (!base64_str) { ... RETURN_FALSE; }' immediately after line 30.

evidence.reason: Attacker-controlled 'data' (parsed at line 14, unconstrained 's' format) is base64-decoded at line 30 with the return status discarded; on malformed input php_base64_decode yields NULL (the fragment itself admits the NULL outcome by guarding efree(base64_str) at lines 70-71). Lines 31-32 then overwrite data_len = base64_str_len (unchecked, declared uninitialized at line 10) and data = base64_str with no success check, and the only guards on the path (lines 18, 24, 29) constrain method/cipher/raw_input, not the decode result. No statement between line 32 and the sink at line 54 validates base64_str/data, so the NULL/garbage-length pair reaches EVP_DecryptUpdate, dereferencing a NULL source pointer (CWE-476 NULL dereference; potential OOB read from the NULL base with the unchecked length). The absent one-statement fix is a NULL/return-status check on base64_str after line 30 before the assignments at lines 31-32.

assumptions: php_base64_decode() returns NULL on malformed/undecodable base64 input; this is the standard failure contract of the callee and is corroborated inside the fragment by the NULL-guarded efree(base64_str) at lines 70-71 (the same variable whose value is forwarded to the sink).
'data', 'method', 'password', and 'iv' are entry-point parameters of the PHP function and are attacker-controlled as per the fragment's inaccessible parse at line 14.
raw_input defaults to 0 (line 3), so the base64 path is reachable without the caller opting in; the caller can also explicitly pass 0.
limitations: Integer overflow of 'outlen = data_len + EVP_CIPHER_block_size(cipher_type)' at line 46, and the resulting emalloc sizing, would require a roughly 2 GiB attacker string (assumed magnitude); not counted as a finding.

The theoretical documented EVP worst case (DecryptUpdate up to inl+block_size plus DecryptFinal up to block_size) versus the 'outlen + 1' allocation at lines 46-47 and the write at line 58 is not concretely derivable: actual plaintext length cannot exceed data_len for the standard ciphers, so no out-of-bounds write is confirmed.
The uninitialized read of base64_str_len at line 10/31 (CWE-457 flavor) is contingent on the same unshown decode-failure contract and is subsumed by the CWE-476 finding.

If a given php_base64_decode implementation never returns NULL, this specific crash path would not trigger; the benchmark pair's one-statement difference (the absent decode-success check) is exactly the fix form whose absence is identified.

verdict.summary: The refresh loop frees entries with `*mdev_types[i]`, which by C precedence indexes the out-parameter pointer `mdev_types` itself rather than the entry array `(*mdev_types)`. With an unconstrained prior count `*nmdev_types >= 2`, iteration i=1 reads past the single pointer cell and wild-dereferences the OOB value as a virMediatedDeviceType*, feeding a garbage pointer to virMediatedDeviceTypeFree.

evidence.reason: Sink at line 11 indexes `mdev_types[i]` (pointer-to-pointer parameter, indexed object capacity 1 established by the fragment's single-deref convention at lines 12 and 18) with i in 0..*nmdev_types-1, where *nmdev_types is an unconstrained size_t input. The loop guard at line 10 (`i < *nmdev_types`) fails the Guard-Identity Audit as wrong-target drift: it bounds i against the entry-array count, not the pointer cell actually indexed, and admits i=1 whenever *nmdev_types >= 2. That reads `mdev_types[1]` out of bounds (CWE-125) and dereferences the resulting garbage before passing it to virMediatedDeviceTypeFree. The absent one-statement fix is the corrected access `virMediatedDeviceTypeFree((*mdev_types)[i]);`.

assumptions: mdev_types points to a single caller-owned virMediatedDeviceTypePtr* variable whose value is the entry-array base; every other in-fragment use is a single `*mdev_types` dereference (lines 12, 13, 18, 19).
*nmdev_types is not constrained by any shown guard and retains the full size_t domain, so the refresh-count value 2 is derivable from the fragment.
limitations: Reaching the failing iteration requires a refresh where the caller previously recorded at least two mdev type entries; a single-entry or empty refresh reaches only i=0 and does not fault.
A NULL-dereference variant (NULL *mdev_types with nonzero count) is not reported: it needs a caller state the fragment does not show.
The capacity of the entry array itself is not shown in the fragment; the finding does not depend on that capacity, only on the pointer cell behind mdev_types.

verdict.summary: Fragment is the patched jfs_evict_inode: diFree(inode) at line 18 is protected by the verbatim NULL guard at line 17 (if (ipimap && JFS_IP(ipimap)->i_imap)), which excludes the NULL ipimap / NULL i_imap failure set on the only path to the sink (check-then-use audit: no mutation between lines 17 and 18; same pointer, same type). The only other dangerous operation, atomic_dec(&bmap->db_active[ji->active_ag]) at line 36, has no demonstrable in-fragment failure: neither the db_active capacity nor a producer of ji->active_ag is shown, so no out-of-range witness is derivable; the `!= -1` guard is not a bound check but the OOB candidate is demoted to a limitation. line 17 `if (ipimap && JFS_IP(ipimap)->i_imap)` short-circuits so both NULL outcomes (ipimap == NULL and JFS_IP(ipimap)->i_imap == NULL) skip diFree at line 18.

The NULL producers for the diFree guard (diMount failure leaving sbi->ipimap or JFS_IP(ipimap)->i_imap NULL) are described by the upstream fix context (commit a53046291020ec) but are not visible inside this fragment; the guard that handles them is verbatim present at line 17.
BUG_ON(!list_empty(&ji->anon_inode_list)) at line 31 is a fail-closed diagnostic abort, which per the class rules is not a finding.
No loop, integer arithmetic, injection, crypto, file/access, or authz sink exists in this fragment.

The out-of-bounds-read variant (array capacity smaller than *nmdev_types, CWE-125) depends on an unshown callee/caller contract violation and is not derivable from the shown code.
A memory leak of the callee's 'types' if virMediatedDeviceGetMdevTypes allocated then returned < 0 (lines 15-16) is a callee-behavior hypothesis, not a confirmed finding.
No injection, crypto, file/access, or SSRF sinks are present in this fragment.

verdict.summary: The vote/consensus parser guards every dangerous operation whose failure set is derivable from the shown statements: the certificate parse is bounded by 'end_of_cert > end_of_header' (line 62), every digest decode is gated by 'strlen(...) != HEX_DIGEST_LEN' plus signed destination sizes, port values are range-bounded in tor_parse_long(...,0,65535,...) with '!ok' rejection, 'smartlist_get(ns->voters, 0)' is preceded by the voters length checks, the signature object copy is bounded to [128,512] by the object_size checks, and all args[] loops use the strict 'i < tok->n_args' bound. No attacker-reachable failing value was found to reach a memory, injection, crypto, or logic sink; the only unverifiable protections are arg-count guarantees supplied by the un-shown tokenizer tables.

assumptions: DIGEST_LEN is 20 and HEX_DIGEST_LEN is 40, so a 40-hex-char string decodes to exactly 20 bytes (relied on by the digest-decode sinks and their strlen guards).

The destination buffers voter->identity_digest, voter->vote_digest, voter->legacy_id_digest, sig->signing_key_digest, and declared_identity are DIGEST_LEN-sized (20 bytes), and sizeof() in the base16_decode calls reflects that.

voter->sigs is initialized at line 208 for every voter created in the K_DIR_SOURCE branch, so all voters reachable via networkstatus_get_voter_by_id have sigs lists; the cleanup path guards voter->sigs with an if-check (line 510).
ns->cert is non-NULL whenever ns->type != NS_TYPE_CONSENSUS: the cert is parsed and NULL-checked at lines 56-63 when ns_type != NS_TYPE_CONSENSUS, and line 79 forces ns->type == ns_type.
token->object_size is bounded in-fragment to [128,512] at line 417 for every K_DIRECTORY_SIGNATURE token before the object_body memdup at line 479.
tor_parse_long's ok flag is the sole validity signal and is checked before every use (lines 102, 125, 129, 182, 235, 239, 379).
limitations: The number of arguments required for header keywords such as published/valid-after/fresh-until/valid-until/client-versions/server-versions/contact/legacy-dir-key is enforced only by the un-shown token tables passed to tokenize_string (lines 29-32, 341); a zero-arg token for those keywords is not producible from the shown statements, so an OOB args[0] read cannot be confirmed or refuted from the fragment alone.

The behavior of helpers find_start_of_next_routerstatus, authority_cert_parse_from_string internals, and routerstatus_parse_entry_from_string (including whether s advances on parse failure) is not shown; a NULL/end-of-string edge from the first and a non-advancing failure in the third (potential CWE-835 infinite loop at line 298) are library-contract hypotheses, not fragment-derivable failures.

Signature verification uses SHA-1 of the document body (line 467, ns_digests.d[DIGEST_SHA1]) and stores unverified consensus signatures (lines 479-480); this is protocol-standard for this Tor era and is not the one-statement fix the pair targets, so it is recorded as an informational note rather than a finding.

Two log_warn calls (lines 161, 187) pass token args to %s unescaped; CR/LF log injection would require a newline inside a single token, which the whitespace-splitting tokenizer does not produce, so no concrete log-injection failure is derivable.

The 'Extraneous token after first directory-signature' check (lines 347-358) and the signature-object size ceiling check (line 475) are present but were not needed to establish safety of the audited sinks; they did not substitute for any missing per-sink guard.

verdict.summary: atusb_disconnect dereferences the result of usb_get_intfdata(interface) without any NULL check. The fragment itself stores NULL into that interface driver-data slot (line 21, usb_set_intfdata(interface, NULL)), so NULL is an admitted value of the slot line 3 reads, and the straight-line path reaches unconditional member accesses (notably line 7, atusb->shutdown = 1...). evidence.reason: First unconditional dereference-write of the pointer 'atusb' obtained at line 3 from 'usb_get_intfdata(interface)'. That lookup's residual range includes NULL: the fragment itself demonstrates NULL is a stored value of this exact interface data slot via line 21 'usb_set_intfdata(interface, NULL);', and no shown statement constrains 'atusb' to non-NULL. Flow is a pure sequence (no conditional exists), so the degenerate witness 'atusb == NULL' passes every (empty) guard set. The fix form that would neutralize this sink is a NULL/equality check on 'atusb' before the use ('if (!atusb) return;' after line 3); it is ABSENT — line 21 executes after the sink and targets the slot, not 'atusb' (wrong-target and wrong-order), so it cannot protect anything. Dereferencing the NULL result yields a write through offset 0 of the object: kernel NULL-pointer dereference, CWE-476.

Dereference of 'atusb' (and 'atusb->usb_dev') reaches the sink before any guard. 'atusb' comes from 'usb_get_intfdata(interface)' at line 3 whose value domain includes NULL — admitted in-fragment because line 21 'usb_set_intfdata(interface, NULL);' writes NULL into the same slot, and no shown constraint excludes it. The path 3->5 is unconditional (no branches). Guard-Identity Audit: no guard exists; the fragment's only NULL-related statement (line 21) is after the sink and does not test the consumed pointer. The absent fix form is the one-statement NULL check ('if (!atusb) return;') after line 3, making this sink's fix form ABSENT; primary evidence remains the unconditional write at line 7.

assumptions: usb_get_intfdata(interface) returns the value previously stored by usb_set_intfdata() for the same interface, including NULL (standard USB API semantics, corroborated in-fragment by line 21 storing NULL).
The atusb members accessed (usb_dev, shutdown, work, rx_urbs, tx_urb, hw) are at non-negative offsets, so a NULL 'atusb' faults on dereference rather than aliasing valid memory.
limitations: The concrete lifecycle event that makes the slot hold NULL at entry (e.g., unbind/re-entry or a partial bind leaving driver data NULL) is orchestrated by the USB core and is not shown in the fragment; the in-fragment demonstration is that a NULL is a legitimate stored value of this slot and the dereference is entirely unguarded.

No other sink (memory corruption, injection, crypto, authz) was found: format strings are literals and no user data reaches any interpretive operation.

verdict.summary: User-controlled fname and backup strings are passed directly as format strings to asprintf (lines 7 and 17), with the attacker-controlled idstring as the sole variadic argument. Format directives such as %s/%x read memory at the idstring pointer and %n writes to the address equal to the idstring pointer value, enabling memory disclosure and corruption. No guard or literal-%s substitution is present.

evidence.reason: Format-string sink (CWE-134): fname is user-controlled per the fragment's own comment at lines 5-6 and has no shown content constraint, so a witness fname="%n" (or %s/%x) reaches the sink directly with no intervening guard; the == -1 check at line 7 only handles allocation failure after the format is interpreted. idstring is the sole variadic argument, so %s/%x read from the idstring pointer and %n writes to the address equal to the idstring pointer value. The absent one-statement fix is a literal "%s" format: asprintf(&logFileName, "%s", fname).

Second format-string sink (CWE-134): backup is user-controlled; the guard at line 10 (backup && *backup) only excludes NULL/empty strings (wrong-target drift) and admits non-empty strings containing format directives, e.g. backup="%n", which reaches line 17 once line 13 admits a regular file. The == -1 check again only handles allocation failure. The absent one-statement fix is asprintf(&suffix, "%s", backup).

assumptions: fname, backup, and idstring are externally supplied entry-point inputs (log-file/backup names and display id string), consistent with the fragment's comment at lines 5-6 that the format string is controlled by the user.
asprintf follows standard printf-family format semantics, including %s/%x reads and %n writes against the variadic argument list.
limitations: The exact privilege context of the X server process is not shown; the fragment's own comment at lines 5-6 states it should never run with elevated privileges, which affects severity calibration but not the confirmed format-string flaw.

A single variadic argument constrains the maximum number of distinct %n targets, but multiple %n plus field-width modifiers can still reuse that argument, and one write primitive suffices for the CWE-134 finding.

Missing one-statement fix: changing the line 16 guard to "if (slot_id >= info->num_memslots)"; the absence yields CWE-125 out-of-bounds read.

assumptions: info->mem_slots has num_memslots_groups rows and num_memslots columns per row; this capacity is established by the access convention of the fragment's own guards at lines 10 and 16, which compare indices against those counts (valid indices 0..count-1).

assumptions: `atoascii` writes at most `out_len - 1` characters plus a terminating NUL, so with `out_len = sizeof(bv) - 1` the produced string length is at most `sizeof(bv) - 2`; this is the bounded-copy convention the fragment's own `- 1` margin relies on.
`nextvar` (line 31) produces NUL-terminated `name`/`value` strings and returns 0 at end of the response buffer.
`snprintf` truncates at `sizeof(b)` and NUL-terminates, keeping line 91's use of `b` safe.
limitations: The `AR` path (`decodearr(value, &narr, lfparr)` line 97, `outputarr(fp, name, narr, lfparr)` line 100) could overflow/over-read `l_fp lfparr[8]` (line 19) if `narr > 8`, but no shown statement bounds `narr` and no shown producer demonstrates an out-of-range count, so no failure is derivable from this fragment.
The internals of `startoutput`, `endoutput`, `output`, `varfmt`, and `nextvar` are unshown; no sink arguments here derive an out-of-domain value from shown code.

The protection's effectiveness depends on `atoascii`'s bounded-copy semantics (an unshown helper convention); if that helper wrote `out_len` bytes the margin would be insufficient, but nothing in the fragment contradicts the standard semantics.

verdict.summary: No confirmed vulnerability. Every dangerous operation with a demonstrable failure set carries a verbatim protective guard: the user-to-user additional_tickets NULL/len==0 check (lines 75-76 with goto out at 82) and the constrained-delegation additional_tickets != NULL && len != 0 gate (lines 739-741) protect both `b->additional_tickets->val[0]` accesses (lines 84, 762); the `s == NULL` guard (lines 138-141, with non-NULL `s = &adtkt.cname` at line 136) protects the `*s` dereference at line 144; and the `num_capath > 0 ?` ternary (line 221) excludes the size_t-underflow OOB read of `capath[--num_capath]`. Remaining candidates (server==NULL in the HDB_ERR_WRONG_REALM branch, unchecked _krb5_principalname2krb5_principal returns feeding krb5_unparse_name, CR/LF log injection) lack a demonstrated in-fragment producer and are demoted to limitations.

assumptions: b->additional_tickets->val has exactly `len` elements (ASN.1 SEQUENCE-OF access convention); the guards at lines 75-76 and 739-741 exclude len==0, so index 0 is in bounds on every admitted path.

_kdc_db_fetch/hdb resolve out-parameters on success (ret == 0): used only to note that objects fetched with a checked ret (client lines 457-458, s4u2self_impersonated_client lines 640-642, krbtgt_out lines 398-399) are non-NULL before their dereferences.
krb5_unparse_name returns an error rather than dereferencing a NULL principal; used only to demote S6/unchecked krb5_make_principal candidates to limitations.
limitations: server->entry.principal->realm at line 180: would be a NULL deref only if _kdc_db_fetch can return HDB_ERR_WRONG_REALM without setting *server; no such in-fragment producer is shown (library-error contract), so this is demoted per the NULL-producer rule.

Unchecked _krb5_principalname2krb5_principal returns at lines 93, 144, 149 feeding krb5_unparse_name at lines 94, 145, 150: failure requires ENOMEM of attacker-fixed small allocations; demoted (unconfirmed CWE-457-style robustness concern).
Unchecked krb5_make_principal returns at lines 236 and 254 (capath and need_referral branches): failure would leave sp NULL but the next krb5_unparse_name is expected to error out; demoted.

Attacker-derived principal-name strings reach kdc_log %s conversions; CR/LF log injection (CWE-117) would require the ASN.1 decoder to admit control octets in component names, which is not shown in the fragment; demoted.
Caller-supplied krbtgt, ticket, replykey NULL-ness is unshown; out of scope.

verdict.summary: In the 0x104 instrument branch, instr[y].size is an attacker-controlled unsigned dword with no minimum; the guard `if (instr[y].size < 29)` admits 0..28, and for size 0..3 the expression `instr[y].size - 4` wraps to >= 0xFFFFFFFC, so `f.read(buffer, 1, instr[y].size - 4)` overflows the 29-byte stack buffer (CWE-121 via CWE-191 underflow). The pattern decompressor additionally indexes `buffer[pc]` with an unvalidated cursor that can exceed the `patdata`-sized heap allocation (CWE-125).

evidence.reason: Attacker-controlled instr[y].size (file dword, line 416, mp_uint32, no shown minimum) passes the only guard, `if (instr[y].size < 29)` (line 418), which admits the failing subset {0,1,2,3}. For size=0 the unsigned subtraction wraps to 0xFFFFFFFC, and f.read copies up to that count — bounded only by file content — into the 29-byte stack buffer declared at line 420 (`mp_ubyte buffer[29];`), overflowing it once the crafted file supplies >= 29 bytes. The absent one-statement fix is a size>=4 validation such as `if (instr[y].size < 4) return MP_LOADER_FAILED;` before line 422; no other statement on the path (411, 418, 433, 438) excludes the witness. Primary CWE-121 stack-based buffer overflow via CWE-191 unsigned underflow.

pc (line 300) is advanced 1..6 bytes per pattern cell with no check against patdata, while buffer is allocated exactly phead[y].patdata bytes (line 288); rows/channum/patdata are independent file fields (lines 263-264, 270-271). With patdata=1, rows=2, channum=1, the second cell reads buffer[pc] with pc >= 1 at line 307, a heap out-of-bounds read; line 341 `memcpy(slot,buffer+pc,5);` can read 5 bytes past the end. The absent fix is a bound check such as `if (pc >= phead[y].patdata) break;` before the access. Primary CWE-125 out-of-bounds read.

assumptions: instr[y].size is a 32-bit unsigned field (read via f.readDwords at line 416).
XMFileBase::read copies up to the requested count, clamped by remaining file data (standard read semantics).
File fields read through f (header, instrument, pattern data, nbu bytes) are attacker-controlled entry-point input; the crafted file supplies the bytes that reach each sink.
Capacities referenced in the fragment: insData[230] (line 3), smpReloc[MP_MAXINSSAMPS] (line 4), nbu[MP_MAXINSSAMPS] (line 5), buffer[29] (line 420), buffer = new [patdata] (line 288).
limitations: smpReloc[nbu[sc]] OOB read (lines 229/232, 595/598): nbu[sc] is a full mp_ubyte 0..255 with no shown validation, but the value of MP_MAXINSSAMPS vs 256 is not derivable from the fragment, so the failing index is convention-dependent.

hdrBuff NULL deref (lines 42-43): hdrsize underflow (line 36) with hdrsize<4 or huge hdrsize yields an enormous allocation; the NULL-checked `new` convention is inferred only from sibling checks at lines 280 and 291, and the behavior of the global operator new is not shown.
MODPLUG message block (lines 777-782): len+1 wraps for len=0xFFFFFFFF, but allocateSongMessage(0)/module->message semantics are not shown.
phead[y].rows*header->channum*6 allocation-size overflow (lines 277/285): a small wrapped allocation could not be demonstrated via an in-fragment factorable rows*channum product.
smp[g+s]/smp[s] writes: the relation between accumulated s and the MP_MAXSAMPLES capacity is not visible in the fragment.
phead/header->ord array capacities are not declared in the fragment; protection rests on clamps at lines 56-59.

verdict.summary: The only dangerous operation with an in-fragment failure set — dereferencing the kzalloc result — is fully protected: 'if (!vch)' (line 9) with 'return ERR_PTR(-ENOMEM);' (line 10) excludes vch==NULL from every path before the dereferences at lines 13/16-21, passing the Guard-Identity Audit (same value, same type, no interleaved mutation). The register-device status is also fail-closed at lines 24-26. No failing value derivable from the shown code survives every guard, so the decisive protective statement is present and no fix statement is absent.

assumptions: vch is the only allocation; its size is fixed by 'kzalloc(sizeof(*vch), GFP_KERNEL)' (line 8).
The comment at line 25 records the intended vch lifetime on the register-error path (freed via virtio_rpmsg_release_device()).
limitations: A NULL dereference of vrp (=vdev->priv) or vrp->vdev at lines 19/21 is not confirmable: no NULL producer for vdev->priv is demonstrated inside the fragment, and validity depends on the unshown caller (probe path).
Whether vch leaks if rpmsg_ctrldev_register_device() fails before wiring the release callback depends on unshown callee behavior; a leak is a robustness concern, not a confirmed security finding.
The fragment contains no memory-copy, injection, crypto, file, or indexing operations, so the audit is limited to NULL and status-handling paths.

verdict.summary: vhost_user_set_inflight_fd maps an attacker-supplied mmap_size (line 67) but never verifies that it covers num_queues * pervq_inflight_size before the loop writes vq->inflight_packed->desc_num / vq->inflight_split->desc_num at addr + i*pervq_inflight_size (lines 90/93, 95), so a large num_queues/queue_size with a small mmap_size produces an out-of-bounds write past the mapped inflight region. The missing one-statement fix is a guard such as if (mmap_size < (uint64_t)pervq_inflight_size * num_queues) return RTE_VHOST_MSG_RESULT_ERR;

evidence.reason: Out-of-bounds write (CWE-787): the store lands at addr + i*pervq_inflight_size, advanced each iteration by line 95, while the object capacity is only the attacker-supplied mmap_size passed to mmap at line 67. num_queues (line 26, uint16_t 0..65535) and queue_size (line 27) come unconstrained from the vhost-user message, so e.g. mmap_size=1, num_queues=65535, queue_size=1024 passes the only guards on the path (line 14 fd count, line 18 msg size/fd>=0, line 69 MAP_FAILED check, line 85 vq NULL check) and the loop stores reach offsets far beyond the 1-page mapping. No guard constrains mmap_size against num_queues*pervq_inflight_size; the absent fix is a pre-loop check such as if (mmap_size < (uint64_t)pervq_inflight_size * num_queues) return RTE_VHOST_MSG_RESULT_ERR;

Same confirmed OOB write (CWE-787) on the split-ring branch: the store targets addr + i*pervq_inflight_size beyond the mmap_size-byte mapping for attacker-controlled num_queues/queue_size/mmap_size (lines 26-27, 24, 67), with all path guards (14, 18, 69, 85) admitting the failing tuple; the decisive pre-loop size guard is absent.

assumptions: mmap_size at line 67 is the capacity of the region written by lines 90/93 (mmap call visible in the fragment).
get_pervq_shm_size_packed/split return a positive per-queue byte size derived from queue_size (name-implied semantics; no cap shown).

mmap rounds the mapping to whole pages, so impacts from crossing the requested mmap_size graduate from silent intra-page overwrite to fault/corruption as the witness span (hundreds of MB) far exceeds one page.
limitations: OOB read of dev->virtqueue[i] at line 84 is not confirmed: the fragment shows no declaration/alloc/capacity for dev->virtqueue, and the line 48-49 access convention only establishes index 0 under dev->nr_vring > 0; a fix checking num_queues vs dev->nr_vring is absent but unconfirmable here.
A non-NULL garbage vq pointer beyond nr_vring leading to arbitrary-store would require unshown heap state (virtqueue slots outside nr_vring are typically NULL and skipped by line 85).
The precise post-bounds impact (silent corruption vs SIGBUS/segfault) depends on adjacent mapping layout, which the fragment never shows.

verdict.summary: Heap buffer overflow in Image::printIFDStructure: the allocation size at line 68 is computed as (long long)(size*count + pad+20) with the product size*count evaluated in 32-bit unsigned arithmetic. For attacker-controlled count (line 37, full uint32, never capped) with a 2-, 4-, or 8-byte type, the product wraps to a small value, so DataBuf buf(allocate) at line 72 allocates as little as 20-24 bytes while the XMP write buf.pData_[count]=0 (line 159) uses the unwrapped count as an index -> heap OOB write (CWE-787); the rational print loop byteSwap4(buf,k*size,...) at lines 105-106 and the ICC out.write(...,count) at line 163 perform heap OOB reads (CWE-125). The guard at line 69-71 (allocate > io.size()) checks the already-wrapped value against the file size and admits the failing inputs. The decisive one-statement fix is absent: the multiplication must be widened (e.g., long long allocate = (long long) size * count + pad + 20;) so the capacity cannot wrap below count.

evidence.reason: Heap OOB write (CWE-787). count is file-derived at line 37 (uint32_t, residual range 0..2^32-1; no cap). With type=LONG -> size=4 (line 60), pad=0 (line 57), count=0x40000001, the line-68 expression (long long)(size*count+pad+20) evaluates size*count in 32-bit arithmetic: 4*0x40000001 = 2^32+4 wraps to 4, so allocate=24 and DataBuf buf(allocate) (line 72) yields a 24-byte buffer. The guard at line 69 (if (allocate > (long long) io.size())) admits this (24 <= any TIFF file size), failing the Guard-Identity Audit because it bounds the wrapped allocation against file size, not count against capacity. bOffsetIsPointer (line 74) is false (count*size wraps to 4) so the read is skipped, and execution reaches line 159 via the isPrintXMP branch (line 158, tag 0x02bc) writing at index 0x40000001 >> 24. Absent fix: 64-bit allocation arithmetic (e.g., long long allocate = (long long) size * count + pad + 20;) or an explicit count < allocate capacity check.

Heap OOB read (CWE-125) from the same 32-bit wrap at line 68. count (line 37) = 0x40000000 with type=RATIONAL -> size=8 (line 61) makes size*count = 2^33 wrap to 0, so allocate=20 (line 68) and buf is 20 bytes (line 72); line 69 admits 20 <= io.size(). kount=5 via line 54 (count>5), and the loop (line 104) admits k=3, whose byteSwap4(buf,3*8+0) reads [24,28) beyond the 20-byte buffer (k=2 already reads [20,24) on line 106). No statement between the allocation (line 72) and the loop constrains k*size against capacity. Absent fix: 64-bit allocation arithmetic so capacity equals the true size*count.

assumptions: Buffer capacity is fixed by the in-fragment allocation: line 72 DataBuf buf(allocate) with allocate from line 68.
typeValid (line 41) admits standard TIFF types LONG(4) and RATIONAL(5); the fragment's own size derivation (lines 58-63) and print branches (lines 97-109) treat them as supported.

isPrintXMP(tag,option) (lines 51, 158) is true for the XMP tag 0x02bc under the structure-printing options the fragment itself handles (kpsBasic/kpsRecursive, line 9); the fragment's own kount selection (line 51) implements the XMP 'haul in all the data' path.
io.size() for any file containing the parsed IFD is at least 20 bytes, so the line-69 check admits the wrapped allocate values 20/24.
limitations: Unbounded recursion (lines 121, 151) and cyclic next-IFD pointers (line 168) can cause stack exhaustion / non-termination DoS; not the one-statement fix under audit.

IPTCNAA branch (lines 127-130) can allocate new byte[count] with a huge raw count because the line-69 check sees only the wrapped size*count, and a short io.read leaves uninitialized bytes consumed by IptcData::printStructure (DoS / uninitialized-read, callee semantics unshown).
io.read return values are unchecked (lines 14, 34, 79, 128, 139, 144, 167), enabling stale/uninitialized dir/buf use on short reads (status-handling, secondary).
Line 163 out.write((const char*)buf.pData_,count) is the same root cause as the primary read finding and not separately evidenced.

verdict.summary: push_pipe() constructs each new pipe_buffer in the fill loop writing only ops/page/offset/len but never initializing the flags member; the uninitialized (stale, on reused ring slots) flags value is published into the pipe ring via pipe->head and is later consumed by pipe_buffer flag logic (e.g., merge/CAN_MERGE semantics), a use-of-uninitialized-variable flaw. The missing one-statement fix is buf->flags = 0;.

evidence.reason: The loop body (line 29) selects the slot at line 30 and, for every executed iteration with alloc_page succeeding (the NULL check at lines 32-33 passes), hand-assembles a new pipe_buffer at lines 35-38 setting only ops, page, offset, len. The flags member is never written anywhere in the fragment, so the buffer's flags is uninitialized/stale (ring slots are reused); the object is published via pipe->head = iter_head; (line 41) and consumed by pipe_buffer flag logic (merge/CAN_MERGE and packet semantics), an uninitialized-use sink (CWE-457). Witness: size >= 1 with an empty, non-full ring and successful alloc_page yields at least one loop-body execution constructing the buffer without flags; no shown guard constrains flags (all guards at lines 11-14, 20-22, 29, 32-33 target size/left/page only - wrong-target drift). The absent one-statement fix is 'buf->flags = 0;' before buf->page = page; (upstream fix 9d2231c5d74e13b2a0546fee6737ee4446017903). Ring indexing itself is bounded by the mask at line 6, so no OOB is claimed.

assumptions: pipe->bufs is the pipe ring of ring_size slots; every index is masked with p_mask = ring_size - 1 (lines 6, 23, 26, 30), bounding indices to [0, ring_size-1].
pipe_buffer.flags is a meaningful member of the pipe_buffer object (absent from the fragment's initializer list) whose consumers sit outside the shown function.
limitations: The downstream consumers of pipe_buffer.flags (pipe_write merge decision, packet/loss/whole handling) are not shown; their exact effect is inferred from standard pipe semantics.
An out-of-bounds write into the ring would require an occupancy invariant (max_usage vs ring_size) not derivable from the fragment; no OOB is asserted.
Whether a given reused slot actually holds a nonzero stale value depends on ring lifetime not shown; the finding is the missing initialization itself (CWE-457), not a specific garbage value.

verdict.summary: vhost_user_set_inflight_fd copies attacker-controlled num_queues (uint16, line 6/23) straight into the loop bound at line 80 and indexes dev->virtqueue[i] at line 81 with no validation that num_queues stays within the device's configured/allocated vring count. A guest can set num_queues up to 65535, causing an out-of-bounds read of the vhost_virtqueue pointer array (CWE-125), leading to crash/DoS and potential information disclosure; the absent fix is a queue-count bound check (e.g., num_queues > dev->max_queue_pairs) before the loop.

evidence.reason: num_queues originates at line 23 (ctx->msg.payload.inflight.num_queues, uint16_t per line 6) with no shown constraint; line 80 admits every i in [0, num_queues-1] up to 65534; line 82's NULL check executes after this load and tests the pointer, not the index (check-then-use / wrong-target drift), so it cannot protect the read. The valid index space is only the device's configured vrings, as shown by the sibling guarded access at line 45-46 (dev->virtqueue[0] only when dev->nr_vring > 0) and the NULL-skip convention at line 82-83. A guest sending num_queues larger than the configured/allocated vring count therefore reads past the virtqueue pointer array (CWE-125). The absent fix form is a validation bounding num_queues to the device's queue-pair capacity before the loop (e.g., if (num_queues > dev->max_queue_pairs) return RTE_VHOST_MSG_RESULT_ERR;), which no statement in the fragment provides.

assumptions: The valid index space of dev->virtqueue[] is bounded by the device's configured vrings; evidenced in-fragment by line 45-46 (dev->virtqueue[0] dereferenced only when dev->nr_vring > 0) and line 82-83 (entries can be NULL).
ctx is guest-supplied vhost-user message data; its payload fields are attacker-controlled entry-point input (lines 14, 15, 21-24).
limitations: The exact allocated size of dev->virtqueue[] and the value of dev->max_queue_pairs are defined outside this fragment (header/device creation), so the precise overflow index beyond the allocated array is not numerically shown; the witness range num_queues > configured vring count is derived from the fragment's own convention.
A subsequent write through an OOB non-NULL garbage vq (lines 86-90) would require unshown heap contents, so arbitrary write is not confirmed.
Writes to desc_num at addr advanced past mmap_size (lines 87/90 vs 92 and line 78) require the guest to supply an undersized mapping and degrade to a fault/DoS, not host memory corruption.
Log writes at lines 16-17/31-39 carry only numeric values plus dev->ifname with no shown CR/LF-capable producer; no log-injection finding.
mmap_size is unbounded in the fragment; large mapping is a resource-exhaustion robustness concern, not a confirmed memory-safety flaw.

verdict.summary: disable_priv_mode fails open: a failed setuid (line 5) is only logged, with exit occurring solely for errno EAGAIN inside an undefined-in-fragment compile-time macro (lines 9-12), and a failed setgid (line 14) is never fatal (line 15). Execution then unconditionally records current_user.euid = current_user.uid (line 17) and current_user.egid = current_user.gid (line 18), so a failed privilege drop leaves the process with elevated effective ids while the privilege-state bookkeeping claims the drop succeeded. The missing one-statement fix is an unconditional exit on setuid/setgid failure (or success-gating the state records).

evidence.reason: Sink: the unconditional privilege-state record. setuid(current_user.uid) at line 5 returns -1 with errno != EAGAIN (e.g., EPERM), admitted by the line 5 branch; line 7 captures errno into e; line 8 logs; the only exit at line 11 is gated by line 10 'if (e == EAGAIN)' and by '#if defined (EXIT_ON_SETUID_FAILURE)' at line 9, which is not defined in the fragment, so the exit excludes only the single errno EAGAIN (coverage drift per Guard-Identity Audit) and fails to fire for the witness; control reaches line 17 and records euid = uid while the effective uid remains privileged. The absent fix form is an unconditional exit on setuid failure or a success-gated record. Primary CWE-754 (fail-open handling of a security-relevant exceptional condition), secondary CWE-269 (improper privilege management).

Sink: the unconditional gid record. setgid(current_user.gid) at line 14 returns -1, admitted by the line 14 branch; line 15 only logs via sys_error with no exit and no state gating, so every failure reaches line 18, which records egid = gid while the effective gid remains privileged. No exit statement exists on the setgid failure path. The absent fix form is a fatal exit on setgid failure (e.g., exit(1)) or a success-gated record. Same mechanism as the primary evidence: CWE-754 fail-open status handling with CWE-269 improper privilege management.

assumptions: current_user.uid/euid/gid/egid are process-global privilege-state fields populated before this function runs; their concrete values are not part of the witness.
Standard POSIX semantics apply: a failed setuid/setgid leaves the effective ids unchanged, so the assignments at lines 17-18 record a drop that did not occur.
The fragment's own < 0 branches (lines 5 and 14) demonstrate that failure of the privilege-drop calls is a reachable, handled control flow.
limitations: A non-EAGAIN setuid failure (the concrete witness) depends on an OS/privilege environment not fully shown, though the fragment's own failure handling and absence of errno filtering admit it; the EAGAIN-only guard would still leave the macro-undefined case failing open.
Downstream consumers of the now-false current_user.euid/current_user.egid are outside this fragment, so the specific privileged operation performed after the failed drop is not demonstrated here.
EXIT_ON_SETUID_FAILURE is not defined within the fragment; credit is not given to line 11's exit because its existence is compile-time conditional and its coverage is limited to EAGAIN.

verdict.summary: In the AR case of cookedprint, decodearr(value, &narr, lfparr) writes an unbounded number of parsed l_fp elements into lfparr (declared with 8 slots at line 19), and outputarr(fp, name, narr, lfparr) reads narr elements. narr is derived from the attacker-controlled 'value' supplied by nextvar and is never bounded to 8, so a value with 9+ comma-separated timestamp tokens triggers a stack out-of-bounds write (CWE-787) and read (CWE-125). The missing one-statement fix is a bound check such as 'narr > (int)COUNTOF(lfparr)' or a capacity argument to decodearr.

evidence.reason: decodearr stores each decoded comma-separated l_fp from the entry-point-supplied 'value' (produced by nextvar at line 31) consecutively into lfparr, whose capacity is 8 elements per the declaration 'l_fp lfparr[8];' (line 19), and reports the count through narr. The only guard on the path is this line's return-status test; it constrains parse success but not the count (wrong-target drift class 3), and no statement between line 97 and 100 bounds narr. An attacker-controlled value with 9 or more tokens yields narr = 9, so the call writes lfparr[8] beyond the 0..7 index span: stack out-of-bounds write, CWE-787. The absent fix is a bound check on narr (e.g., '|| narr > (int)COUNTOF(lfparr)') or passing lfparr's capacity into decodearr.

outputarr iterates over narr elements of lfparr, which holds only 8 elements (line 19). narr is the unbounded count returned by decodearr from the attacker-controlled value and is not checked before this use, so narr = 9 reads lfparr[8] out of bounds: CWE-125. The absent fix is a bound check on narr before the call (e.g., 'else if (narr <= (int)COUNTOF(lfparr))').

assumptions: lfparr capacity = 8 elements, established by the visible declaration 'l_fp lfparr[8];' (line 19).
decodearr's standard semantics with the shown arguments: count of successfully decoded comma-separated l_fp tokens stored consecutively into lfparr, return value 1 on success.
atoascii honors its shown in_len/out_len arguments (standard helper semantics), which supports the PRESENT resolution of the bv append sink at lines 122-123.
nextvar treats data as an entry-point (server-supplied) source of name/value pairs with no visible cap on the number of tokens inside a value.
limitations: decodearr's internal implementation is not shown; if it silently capped its own writes at 8, the in-call write would not overflow, but such an invisible cap is not credited per the verifiability rule, and narr would still be unbounded at the outputarr read (line 100).
MAXVARLEN/MAXVALLEN numeric values are not defined in the fragment; they are irrelevant to the confirmed AR-chain finding.
output() is treated as a formatting output call; no injection claim is made on it.

verdict.summary: PresentationContext_new caps the derived allocation size before use: 's = width * height * 4ULL' (line 8) is immediately bounded by 'if (s > INT32_MAX) return NULL;' (lines 9-10), and the same unchanged 's' is the only size argument to BufferPool_Take (line 31). The guard passes the Guard-Identity Audit (same value, same size_t type, no interleaved mutation), so the only in-fragment-confirmable dangerous sink failure set (oversized attacker-derived allocation size) is fully excluded. The residual 32-bit wrap of 'width * height' before the 4ULL promotion would corrupt 's' to a small value whose overflow impact depends entirely on unshown decode-path writes, and is therefore demoted to a limitation.

assumptions: UINT32 is an unsigned 32-bit type, so 'width * height' at line 8 is computed in unsigned 32-bit arithmetic before the '4ULL' promotion (making the wrap candidate at line 8 real but its impact not in-fragment).
INT32_MAX == 2^31-1 and size_t is at least 32-bit, so 's > INT32_MAX' at line 9 is well-defined and equals the shown 2 GiB cap.
BufferPool_Take(priv->surfacePool, s) uses s as the requested buffer size and its NULL failure is handled at lines 24-27.
width/height/x/y are caller-supplied UINT32 values with no shown constraints; s is the derived value actually consumed by the allocation.
limitations: If width*height >= 2^32, the product wraps in 32-bit at line 8 (e.g., 65536*65536 -> s=0), so the lines 9-10 cap compares a wrapped value; the undersized surfaceData could only be overflowed by unshown decode/present-path writes, which is outside the fragment, so this is not confirmable as a finding.
video->priv at line 6 is dereferenced without a NULL check; a NULL video could only come from an unshown caller.
Return values of h264_context_reset (line 21) and yuv_context_reset (line 45) are ignored; their internal capacity handling is unshown.
The cap deliberately admits allocations up to INT32_MAX (~2 GiB); OOM at that budget is the intended limit rather than an in-fragment overflow.

verdict.summary: The fragment is the fixed member of the pair. The only sink with a demonstrable failure geometry is the double lbr_chartabsize_adv advance at lines 161-164, which would read past the NUL terminator if a line ended in a backslash. That failure is neutralized by the verbatim guard 'if (*that == '\\' && *(that+1) != NUL)' (line 160): it checks the exact character consumed by the second advance (same pointer, same type, no interleaved mutation), admits only lines where the backslash has a non-NUL follower, and under both guard outcomes the pointer lands at or before the in-bounds NUL so the loop re-check at line 143 terminates safely. verdict.summary: disable_priv_mode never makes a failed privilege drop fatal: the setuid path exits only on EAGAIN and only when the unshown macro EXIT_ON_SETUID_FAILURE is defined, the setgid path only calls sys_error, and lines 25-26 unconditionally record euid/egid as dropped. Any other syscall failure therefore leaves the process with effective root while current_user.euid/egid claim privileges were dropped — a fail-open privilege-drop (CWE-754).

evidence.reason: A setresuid/setuid failure admitted by `if (setresuid (...) < 0)` / `if (setuid (current_user.uid) < 0)` (lines 6/8) is handled only by `e = errno;` (line 11) and the diagnostic `sys_error (...)` (line 12); termination exists solely for `e == EAGAIN` (line 14) under the unshown macro `#if defined (EXIT_ON_SETUID_FAILURE)` (line 13). Every other errno (e.g. EPERM) falls through to this unconditional write on line 25, which records euid == uid although the kernel effective uid is unchanged (setuid failure leaves euid intact). The absent fix form is an unconditional fatal action on any failure (e.g. unguarded `exit (e);`) before this state write, or gating the write on success. This is a fail-open privilege drop: CWE-754.

A setresgid/setgid failure admitted by `if (setresgid (...) < 0)` / `if (setgid (current_user.gid) < 0)` (lines 19/21) is handled only by the diagnostic `sys_error (...)` (line 23) with no exit or return for any errno, so control always reaches line 26, which records egid == gid although the kernel effective gid remains privileged. The absent fix form is an exit/return on setgid failure before this write, or gating the write on success. Same fail-open privilege-drop mechanism: CWE-754.

assumptions: disable_priv_mode runs in a privileged (e.g., setuid-root) process whose purpose is to drop privileges; on failure, standard setresuid/setresgid semantics leave the effective uid/gid unchanged.
current_user.euid/egid are the program's global credential bookkeeping consumed by later security decisions; those consumers are not shown.

sys_error is treated as diagnostic (print-and-continue): the fragment's own conditional EAGAIN exit at lines 13-16 shows that reaching a later statement is the intended normal outcome, and no shown statement attributes fail-closed behavior to sys_error.
limitations: The concrete OS conditions that make setresuid/setresgid return < 0 (e.g., EPERM/EAGAIN) are environment-dependent and not shown; the finding rests on the fragment itself admitting failure via its `< 0` checks and then mishandling it.
The definedness of EXIT_ON_SETUID_FAILURE is not shown; even at its strongest reading, the EAGAIN-only exit leaves all other errno values and the entire gid failure path unprotected.
The downstream privileged-sensitive action performed while the process still holds effective root is outside the fragment, so impact is stated at the credential-state level.

verdict.summary: warnf() reads out of bounds of the 256-byte print_buffer when a warning message contains no whitespace and is long enough to truncate (len > 255): the inner scan bottoms out at cut == 0, ptr advances by cut+1 while len -= cut leaves len unchanged, so ptr walks past the buffer and ptr[cut] over-reads stack memory, which is then written to config->errors; the outer while(len>0) loop also never terminates.

evidence.reason: OOB read (CWE-125): fmt/varargs are unconstrained (no shown call site, category (c)); vsnprintf at line 11 returns the would-be length (e.g., 300) for a whitespace-free expansion, filling char print_buffer[256] (declared line 7) with 255 non-space bytes. Line 18 admits len=300. Each iteration the scan finds no space, exits with cut==0, line 27 advances ptr by 1 while line 28 (len -= cut) leaves len unchanged, so the outer while(len>0) at line 15 never terminates and ptr advances past index 255; at iteration 179 ptr[cut] reads print_buffer[256], one past the declared capacity. No guard bounds ptr or cut when cut==0; the absent fix is a statement forcing a safe cut (e.g., if(cut == 0) cut = WARN_TEXTWIDTH-1;) or bounding ptr within sizeof(print_buffer), and the over-read bytes are emitted to config->errors, also causing non-termination (CWE-835).

Same confirmed mechanism as line 21: once ptr has advanced past print_buffer's end (guaranteed because cut==0 leaves len unchanged at line 28 and ptr advances every iteration at line 27), fwrite reads cut+1 out-of-bounds bytes from ptr and writes them to config->errors (stack-data disclosure, CWE-125). The absent fix is the same one-statement guard/bound; no shown statement constrains ptr to the buffer.

assumptions: print_buffer capacity is exactly 256 bytes (declared at line 7), valid indices 0..255.
WARN_TEXTWIDTH is a small positive constant (standard curl value 79); its exact value only shifts the iteration at which the first out-of-bounds access occurs (any value >= 1 preserves the failure).
ISSPACE follows standard isspace semantics, so NUL (index 255 after truncation) is not treated as whitespace, preventing an early stop.
vsnprintf returns the would-be written length on truncation (standard semantics), so len can exceed 255 while the buffer holds only 255 chars plus NUL.
limitations: The specific failing input (a whitespace-free warning message of length >= 256) is supplied by a caller not shown in the fragment; provenance is the unconstrained parameter domain (category (c)), so the chain's first link is assumed rather than shown.
The duplicate va_start at lines 9-10 is undefined behavior in principle, but no concrete memory-safety failure is demonstrable from the shown code, so it is not reported as a finding.
Any crash versus continued garbage reads depends on stack layout/contents beyond the buffer, which is not asserted.
The fputs(ptr, config->errors) at line 31 in the else branch is NUL-terminated and bounded by the buffer, so it is not treated as a sink.

The fragment already contains defensive statements (rawsize == 0 check at lines 81-83 protecting the division at line 405; maxrlvls < 1 at line 376), but neither constrains the index at lines 283-284 on the overflowing path.

Capacity is established by the fragment: newp = malloc (end_name - dirname) at line 474 (and alloca_account (end_name - dirname, alloca_used) at lines 470-471). For block[0] in 33..255 the copy size 33..255 exceeds the block payload bound the fragment itself enforces in the sibling cases (guard at line 138, clamp at lines 156-157, assignment at line 128). No guard on this path constrains block[0]: lines 138-139 and 153-157 protect different switch cases (Guard-Identity Audit wrong-target drift, class 3), and the `dma_size != 0` check at line 193 runs after the copy. Absent fix: `if (data->block[0] > I2C_SMBUS_BLOCK_MAX) return -EINVAL;` (or clamp to I2C_SMBUS_BLOCK_MAX) in the I2C_SMBUS_BLOCK_DATA write branch before lines 119/124, mirroring lines 138-139.

assumptions: data->block[0] is an attacker-controlled SMBus block length byte (entry-point input via the i2c-dev/user-space SMBus transaction); the fragment imposes no constraint on it on the I2C_SMBUS_BLOCK_DATA write path.

Caller-side validation outside the fragment (e.g., in i2c-dev or the i2c core) is not shown and was not assumed; no such constraint is demonstrated, so the length byte is treated as unconstrained per the entry-point rule.

Sibling BLOCK_PROC_CALL path (line 148) writes up to dma_buffer[1..32] while only I2C_SMBUS_BLOCK_MAX (32) bytes are DMA-mapped (line 141); no memory-safety impact is demonstrable from the shown code because the backing buffer capacity is unshown, so it is recorded as a limitation rather than a finding.

verdict.summary: decode_errcode_attr() computes value.slen = attr->hdr.length - 4 without any minimum-length validation. attr->hdr.length is attacker-controlled network data read by GETATTRHDR(buf, &attr->hdr) at line 13 and is unconstrained in the fragment, so length < 4 underflows value.slen to a negative value (−4..−1) that is handed to pj_strdup(pool, &attr->reason, &value) at line 22 as an attacker-chosen copy count (huge once interpreted as an unsigned size), producing an out-of-bounds read from value.ptr = buf + 8. The decisive one-statement fix — a length check such as 'if (attr->hdr.length < 4) return PJ_STUN_EINVALIDLEN;' before the subtraction — is absent.

evidence.reason: Taint: buf is entry-point network/STUN data; GETATTRHDR(buf, &attr->hdr) at line 13 imports attr->hdr.length (pj_uint16_t) from buf[2..3] with no shown constraint, leaving its full domain 0..65535. Sink: pj_strdup copies value.slen bytes from value.ptr (= buf + 8, line 18); value.slen is derived at line 19 as attr->hdr.length - 4 after int promotion, so for length in {0..3} it is -4..-1 (a huge count once passed to the copy's unsigned size), and for length up to 65535 it is up to 65531. The fragment is branch-free — no guard, bound, or validation sits on the straight path line 13 -> line 19 -> line 22 — so the degenerate witness length = 0 (attacker sets buf[2..3] = 0, which the fragment never excludes) reaches the copy with value.slen = -4 (CWE-190 underflow) and reads out of bounds beyond the received attribute region (CWE-125). Fix-Presence ledger for this sink: ABSENT — the neutralizing minimum-length guard (e.g., 'if (attr->hdr.length < 4) return PJ_STUN_EINVALIDLEN;') or an equivalent slen >= 0 / bounded-copy validation is not present anywhere in the fragment.

assumptions: buf points at attacker-controlled STUN ERROR-CODE attribute data; the fragment's own unconditional reads of buf[0..3] (line 13), buf[6..7] (line 15), and buf+8 (line 18) establish an access convention that buf covers at least the 8 fixed attribute bytes.
attr->hdr.length is pj_uint16_t (0..65535) as set by the GETATTRHDR macro, and value.slen is a signed pj_ssize_t; the expression length - 4 is computed in int before assignment.

pj_strdup's name-implied contract is a length-driven byte copy (memcpy with the supplied slen converted to an unsigned count at the copy), so a negative slen acts as a near-SIZE_MAX count; the callee body itself is not shown.
limitations: The receiving message buffer's exact capacity is not declared in the fragment, so the concrete number of bytes read past the end of the buffer is transport-dependent; the confirmed defect is the unchecked attacker-controlled length reaching the copy (count up to 65531, or the underflowed huge count), not an in-fragment leaf capacity.

The copy also systematically overruns the attribute's own region by 4 bytes (ptr at offset 8 but slen = length - 4 instead of length - 8), though whether those 4 bytes are outside the allocated buffer depends on trailing message data not shown.

If pj_strdup internally skips non-positive lengths, the length < 4 case instead stores a negative slen / NULL ptr in the returned attribute while the discarded pj_strdup status and full PJ_SUCCESS are still returned — downstream consumption is out of fragment scope.
buf[6]/buf[7] and GETATTRHDR reads are not findings: an OOB would require buffer capacity < 8, contradicting the fragment's own unconditional accesses.
The discarded pj_strdup return (CWE-754 style) has no demonstrable in-fragment security consumer, so it is recorded as a limitation, not a confirmed finding.

verdict.summary: Guest-controlled uint16_t num_queues and queue_size (read at lines 40-41 with no validation) drive the mmap size at line 53-54 and the memset at line 60; the maximum admitted values (65535 x 65535) request and zero a multi-GB region and run up to ~4.29e9 loop iterations, enabling host resource exhaustion. The host mmap may succeed for multi-GB sizes under default overcommit, making the line 60 memset and the line 79-85 loop reachable; otherwise the line 55 error path is taken.

The exact ~6.8e10-byte magnitude depends on the unshown per-VQ size helper output and OS mmap/overcommit limits; the finding rests on a sound range analysis with that magnitude assumption, hence confidence 0.67.
The 4.29e9-iteration loop (lines 79-85) is a CPU-consuming consequence of the same missing cap but is not a separate memory-safety failure.

verdict.summary: fill_threshhold_buffer copies data with three memcpy calls (lines 9, 13, 17) whose byte counts left_width, src_width, and right_width are int parameters constrained by no in-fragment validation; a negative size converts to a size_t near SIZE_MAX and a large positive cumulative write (left_width + num_tiles*src_width + right_width) is never capped against the destination. A negative src_width (e.g., -1) admitted by the loop condition is converted by memcpy's size_t parameter to a value near SIZE_MAX, reading far past src_strip and writing far past dest_strip, and positive src_width accumulates unchecked across num_tiles iterations against the finite destination convention established by the sequential writes. No validation or bounded-copy substitution precedes this sink; the absent fix form is an input-validation guard on src_width (and cumulative length) before the copy, giving an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787).

left_width and left_offset are int parameters with no in-fragment constraint (residual range INT_MIN..INT_MAX). A negative left_width converts to a near-SIZE_MAX size_t in memcpy, causing an out-of-bounds write to dest_strip and an out-of-bounds read from src_strip + left_offset; a large positive left_width with left_offset makes the copied span exceed the source object and the cumulative dest write exceed the destination convention. No validation statement (e.g., non-negative/in-range left_width and left_offset, or a checked copy) exists on any path to this sink — resolver ABSENT; primary CWE-787.

right_width is an unconstrained int (residual range INT_MIN..INT_MAX) with no guard of any kind on the path to this copy. A negative right_width becomes a near-SIZE_MAX size_t copy and a large positive right_width extends the cumulative write (left_width + num_tiles*src_width + right_width) past the destination convention, an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787) plus out-of-bounds read of src_strip. The absent one-statement fix is an input-validation/bounds check on right_width before the memcpy; no such statement is present.

assumptions: dest_strip and src_strip are finite, caller-allocated buffers; the function's own sequential writes establish the destination access convention of left_width + num_tiles*src_width + right_width bytes.

The size/count parameters are caller-supplied and, in the surrounding image/file-processing subsystem, would derive from external data; the fragment itself shows no trusted invariant that forces them non-negative or in-range.
The PACIFY_VALGRIND block (lines 18-23) is diagnostic-only and not part of the data-copy path.

If an unshown caller always supplied non-negative, in-range sizes, the copies would behave; no such invariant is visible in the shown code, and the prompt forbids assuming it.
A fully fragment-internal capacity proof (Phase 4 OOB rule) is unavailable because no allocation/sizeof appears; this bounds confidence to the range-analysis band rather than an exact-witness band.

Same buffer-overflow chain as line 502: for dirname `~a\b/cd` (capacity 4 from line 474), `p` has advanced past the end during the unescape loop and this NUL-termination write lands at `newp[5]`, a second out-of-bounds byte. Other inventoried sinks were audited and resolved PRESENT or exact-fit (gl_pathv init guarded by line 41; brace buffer exact fit at lines 91-97/103/144; dirname prefix lines 263-268; home concat lines 416-432; pw_dir concat lines 549-566; '~' answer block guarded by line 594; GLOB_MARK strcpy exact fit; strdup NULL check line 380; getpwnam_r `p` check line 539) — these do not affect the verdict, which is decided by the least-protected sink.
No lower-confidence candidates (integer overflow of `home_len + dirlen`, non-termination, etc.) were confirmed from the shown statements; they remain out of scope.

verdict.summary: extract_archive_thread creates symbolic links whose target is taken verbatim from the attacker-controlled archive (archive_entry_symlink at line 220) with no validation confining it to extract_data->destination. verdict.summary: The only security-relevant sink is the abort-packet builder called at lines 10-11, whose length argument is sizeof(err_str). Because err_str is the local static array declared at line 8, sizeof yields exactly its 40-byte capacity (39 characters plus the NUL terminator); the admitted length set is {40}, excluding every out-of-range value on the single straight-line path, so no failing length can reach the callee's copy. limitations: Any callee behavior beyond copying exactly err_len bytes (e.g., writing a terminator one byte past the payload, or reinterpreting the error text) is not shown and was not assumed; no finding is derived from it.
Downstream consumption of the transmitted error text (peer-side processing or logging) is outside the shown fragment and unconfirmed.

No demonstrated failing value exists for this fragment: the length argument is a compile-time constant equal to the array capacity, so the degenerate test set (0, -1, INT_MIN/INT_MAX, SIZE_MAX) is excluded by construction.

verdict.summary: ReadBMPImage is internally guarded on every dangerous sink. No shell/query/URL/format-injection, crypto, or file/access-control sinks are present in the shown fragment; the `1.5*` and extent guards are the decisive protections for the memory sinks.
